newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: First assisted suicide divides Australia.
newsitem.headline: First assisted suicide divides Australia.

text.p: Australia was divided on Thursday by news from the outback of the world's first legal assisted suicide, with church leaders crying shame and a leading politician describing it as "beautiful."
Bob Dent, a terminally ill, prostate cancer patient in his mid-60s, died on Sunday by a computer-delivered lethal injection after persuading doctors that he had nothing to live for.

"I was, and still am, deeply ashamed that Australia should be the only country in the world to legalise the killing of an innocent person," Sydney's Roman Catholic archbishop Edward Clancy told a news conference.
"Respect, reverence for human life is a cornerstone of our civilisation," Clancy added. "When that goes, our society begins to unravel."
But Victoria State premier Jeff Kennett, a supporter of voluntary euthanasia, welcomed Dent's death and said moves to have the Northern Territory's suicide law quashed were immoral.
"For people to be able to die with grace and dignity at their choosing as opposed to suffering is just beautiful," Kennett told reporters.
"Life is about choice; death should be about choice and politicians ought to butt out," he said.
Nitschke said Dent had reassured him as he died, telling him that was he was doing was "an act of love."

Dent's death was overseen by Darwin doctor Philip Nitschke, who called in an eminent psychiatrist from Sydney for final approval because local psychiatrists would not sign the legal documents for the suicide to go ahead.
The psychiatrist, John Ellard, said Dent had been fully aware of what he was doing.
"I found an intelligent and sensitive man, fully aware of all the issues concerning him and his illness," Ellard said.
"I had no hesitation in signing the necessary documents under the relevant act," he added.

The Northern Territory law, which came into operation almost three months ago, has been widely condemned. It is opposed by Prime Minister John Howard, who is backing a move to quash it in federal parliament, and by the Vatican.
It has also been condemned by indigenous Aborigines, who hold life to be sacred.
Clancy said that Aborigines, immigrants and elderly people would be the ones to suffer if euthanasia were allowed to take hold and society's most vulnerable were pressured to end their own lives.
Aboriginal officials contacted in Darwin declined to comment out of respect for Dent, saying that the issue was no longer hypothetical but had become a reality.
